Development of an End-to-End Image-Based 9x9 Sudoku Solver Integrating Adaptive Thresholding and Convolutional Neural Networks for Automated Digit Recognition

Luigi T. Cuansing\*1, Nicholaus P. Narte\#2, Jian Enrico T. Ng Suy\*3, Anton Rafael T. Tan\#4

*Department of Electronics, Computer, and Electrical Engineering*  
*De La Salle University \- Manila, 2401 Taft Ave., Malate, Manila, Philippines*

`1luigi_cuansing@dlsu.edu.ph`

`2nicholaus_narte@dlsu.edu.ph`

`3jian_ngsuy@dlsu.edu.ph`

`4anton_tan@dlsu.edu.ph`

***Abstract*****—** This project develops an end-to-end image-based 9×9 Sudoku solver that automatically detects a Sudoku grid in a photograph, corrects perspective distortion, segments and preprocesses each cell through adaptive thresholding and shape-based cleanup, recognizes the digits with a convolutional neural network (CNN), and reconstructs and solves the puzzle with a constraint-propagation solver augmented by a confidence-aware correction search. The CNN (double-convolution architecture with global average pooling, 289,520 parameters) was trained on synthetic print-font digits, MNIST/EMNIST handwritten digits, synthetic empty cells, and 52,685 real photo cells under a sealed 70/15/15 data partition. On the sealed 210-photograph test set, the system achieves 98.44% digit accuracy, 99.76% empty-cell accuracy, and 90.0% exact puzzle reconstruction; end-to-end, 87.6% of grids are auto-detected with 91.63% digit accuracy on detected grids. The results show that for cascade tasks of this type, recognition accuracy and confidence calibration are the binding constraints, not the solver.  
***Keywords***—Sudoku solver, adaptive thresholding, convolutional neural network, digit recognition, constraint propagation, image processing

1. # Introduction

Sudoku is a logic-based number placement puzzle that consists of a 9×9 grid divided into nine 3×3 subgrids. The objective is to fill the empty cells with digits from 1 to 9 such that each row, column, and subgrid contains every digit exactly once \[1\]. While numerous digital Sudoku solvers are available, users are generally required to manually encode the puzzle before obtaining a solution. This process can be time-consuming and inconvenient, particularly for puzzles captured from printed media.

Recent advancements in computer vision and deep learning have enabled the automation of image analysis and digit recognition tasks. Computer vision techniques can detect and isolate Sudoku grids from images, while image preprocessing methods such as adaptive thresholding improve image quality by minimizing the effects of uneven lighting and shadows. Furthermore, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated high accuracy in recognizing handwritten and printed digits, making them well suited for optical digit recognition applications \[2\], \[3\].

This project, \*Development of an End-to-End Image-Based 9×9 Sudoku Solver Integrating Adaptive Thresholding and Convolutional Neural Networks for Automated Digit Recognition\*, aims to develop a complete system that automatically solves Sudoku puzzles from images. The proposed system first identifies and extracts the Sudoku grid using computer vision techniques, segments the grid into individual cells, and preprocesses each cell through adaptive thresholding. To improve the robustness of Sudoku grid detection, the computer vision module is developed and evaluated using the \*\*Sudoku Box Detection\*\* dataset from Kaggle, which contains annotated images of Sudoku puzzles under varying orientations, lighting conditions, and backgrounds \[4\]. The extracted digit images are then processed by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to recognize the existing numbers, after which the recognized puzzle is reconstructed digitally and solved automatically using a backend Sudoku-solving algorithm.

By integrating image preprocessing, digit recognition, and puzzle solving into a single workflow, the project demonstrates the practical application of computer vision and deep learning in automating structured image analysis. In addition to providing an efficient Sudoku-solving tool, the developed system illustrates techniques that can be extended to applications such as document digitization, optical character recognition, and intelligent form processing.

2. # Design and Application

This section discusses the objectives of the study and the flowchart of the system.

1. ## *Objectives*

The primary objective of the project is to develop an end-to-end image-based Sudoku solver that automatically recognizes and solves a standard 9×9 Sudoku puzzle using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Specifically, the project aims to:

1. To isolate and extract individual cells from a Sudoku image using computer vision techniques, specifically thresholding.  
2. To train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to predict the missing digits.  
3. To integrate both phases into a complete, end-to-end automated solver.

   2. ## *Flowchart of System*

Figure 1 shows the overall workflow of the proposed system. The process begins with capturing or loading an image containing a Sudoku puzzle. The image then undergoes preprocessing, where the Sudoku grid is detected, corrected for perspective distortion, and segmented into 81 individual cells. Each cell is processed through adaptive thresholding to produce high-contrast images suitable for digit recognition.

The preprocessed cell images are subsequently passed to the trained CNN model, which identifies the digits present in each cell while distinguishing empty cells from occupied ones. The recognized digits are combined to reconstruct the Sudoku puzzle in digital form. Finally, the completed puzzle is generated using the solving module, and the solution is displayed to the user.

4. # Results and Discussion

   1. ## *Evaluation Setup*

The system was evaluated on the official labeled test partition of the Lexski/sudoku-image-recognition dataset \[4\]: 210 real photographs of Sudoku puzzles, sealed at a fixed 70/15/15 partition of the full 1,400-image dataset so that no test image is ever used for training. Ground truth consists of definite cell labels (digits 1–9 or empty) plus keypoints marking the grid corners. The final CNN — a double-convolution network with global average pooling (48×48 input, 289,520 parameters) — was trained for 21 epochs (early-stopped at best validation score 0.9933) on synthetic print-font digits, MNIST/EMNIST handwritten digits, synthetic empty cells, and 52,685 real photo cells extracted from the sealed train partition, with temperature calibration (T = 1.162) fitted on the photo validation partition.

Every metric below was produced by the project's own labeled benchmark harness. Each puzzle is evaluated in two modes: **recognition** (grid warped from the ground-truth corners, isolating digit recognition and solving) and **end-to-end** (grid auto-detected from the photograph with contour- and line-based detection, measuring the deployed behavior).

   2. ## *Recognition Performance*

On the sealed 210-puzzle test, the final model achieves 98.73% definite-cell accuracy (11,269/11,414), 98.44% digit accuracy on the 8,888 solved (digit) cells, and 99.76% empty-cell accuracy (Table 1). Of the 210 puzzles, 189 (90.0%) are reconstructed exactly on their definite cells. Per-digit accuracy is uniformly high (96.6%–99.2%, Table 2), with no dominant confusion pair.

*Table 1 — Recognition-mode metrics on the sealed 210-puzzle test (ground-truth corners).*

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Definite-cell accuracy | 98.73% (11,269/11,414) |
| Digit accuracy (solved cells) | 98.44% (8,749/8,888) |
| Empty-cell accuracy | 99.76% (2,520/2,526) |
| Exact grids (definite cells) | 90.0% (189/210) |
| No-duplicate grids (full 81-cell) | 21.0% (44/210) |
| Solve rate (valid solution, bounded correction) | 18.6% (39/210) |
| gt-preserving solves | 0.5% (1/210) |
| Solver nodes (mean / max / limit hits) | 22,378 / 203,287 / 13 |
| Cells re-sensed | 5,552 |

*Table 2 — Per-digit accuracy on solved cells (recognition mode).*

| Digit | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy (%) | 96.6 | 98.8 | 98.9 | 98.8 | 98.4 | 98.0 | 98.4 | 99.2 | 98.8 |

The confidence report shows that of the 145 wrong cells, only 34 (23%) carry confidence above 0.9 (Case B) and 28 below 0.5 (Case A); the temperature calibration moves the error mass into low-confidence cells that the solver's correction search can revisit.

   3. ## *End-to-End Performance*

With automatic grid detection, 184 of the 210 photographs (87.6%) yield a detected grid (contour-based 183, line-based 1). On detected grids, definite accuracy is 93.03%, digit accuracy 91.63%, and empty accuracy 97.74%; 72.8% of detected puzzles are reconstructed exactly and 15.8% are solved within the correction budget (Table 3).

*Table 3 — End-to-end metrics on the sealed 210-puzzle test (auto grid detection).*

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Grid detection | 87.6% (184/210) |
| Definite-cell accuracy (detected) | 93.03% |
| Digit accuracy (detected) | 91.63% |
| Empty-cell accuracy (detected) | 97.74% |
| Exact grids (of detected) | 72.8% (134/184) |
| Solve rate (of detected) | 15.8% (29/184) |

   4. ## *Discussion*

The cascade constraint dominates the results: a puzzle with roughly 27 givens is solvable only if every given is recognized correctly, so ~99% per-digit accuracy is a precondition for reliable solving. At 98.44% digit accuracy, 90.0% of puzzles are recognized exactly, yet only 18.6% solve within the change budget — a single wrong clue typically makes the puzzle unsolvable within the bounded correction search. The candidate-only-cell diagnostic (4,205 of 5,596 candidate cells read as digits, which the solver may treat as false clues) and the oracle (only 3 of 164 failed puzzles solve when those cells are emptied) together show that the remaining failures are genuine recognition errors concentrated in non-definite cells, not solver defects.

The gap between recognition and end-to-end performance (98.73% vs. 93.03% definite) is attributable to grid detection: 26 of 210 photographs fail detection entirely, and warps from imperfect detection stress the same preprocessing and recognition stages. Per-position analysis shows recognition accuracy is flat across the grid, confirming the CNN has no positional bias.

The iterative development measured every stage change on the same labeled benchmark: preprocessing redesign raised empty-cell accuracy from 54.3% (legacy) to 99.8% (final pipeline); the architecture/calibration change plus photo-domain training raised sealed-test digit accuracy from 84.44% (synthetic-only) to 98.44% (final model), cutting wrong cells from 1,393 to 145.

5. # Recommendations

Future work should focus on the three measured bottlenecks in order of impact:

1. **Grid detection.** 12.4% of photographs (26/210) fail detection; improving robustness to curved pages, heavy shadows, and partial grids directly raises end-to-end performance.
2. **Non-definite (candidate-only) cells.** These cells are read as digits in large numbers (4,205/5,596) and reach the solver as potential false clues; a confidence-aware gate that treats them as releases rather than givens is the most promising solver-side improvement.
3. **Recognition headroom.** Per-digit accuracy above 99% is the target set by the cascade constraint; larger photo corpora, stronger augmentation, and sequence-based models (e.g., CRNN) are directions worth exploring.

6. # Conclusions

This project developed and measured an end-to-end image-based 9×9 Sudoku solver integrating adaptive thresholding, shape-based cell cleanup, a convolutional neural network for digit recognition, confidence calibration, and a constraint-propagation solver with a confidence-aware correction search. On the sealed 210-photograph test partition, the system recognizes 98.44% of digits and 99.76% of empty cells, reconstructs 90.0% of puzzles exactly, and solves 18.6% within its correction budget; end-to-end from the photograph, 87.6% of grids are detected. The study demonstrates that for cascade tasks of this type, recognition accuracy and calibration — not solver cleverness — are the binding constraints, and that each pipeline stage must be measured, not assumed.
